## A) Taking the most eye‑catching page in **service grid** as the general representative of the entire material, ignoring other columns
**Decision: can only be partially retained**

**[Box 1 — Why people want this]**  
The diagrams are visually “complete” (especially **P4 Reference framework** or **P6 Value chain/capabilities**) and look like they already summarize everything: blocks, arrows, icons, “platform/content/customer experience”.

**[Box 2 — Narrow conditions where it can stand]**  
It can stand **only** as an **entry thumbnail** for the set **if** it is explicitly labeled “overview only” and it has mandatory links to the other columns/pages (at minimum to **P5, P9, P10**). In other words: it can represent **navigation**, not represent **coverage**.

**[Box 3 — What’s missing / which column gets damaged]**  
- Missing: **time-point control and pass conditions** that exist in **online track** (P7 lifecycle, P9 stages).  
- Missing: explicit **cost/budget** anchor from **charging beads** (P10 “Estimated Budget”; P7 “Billing and Revenue Management”).  
- Damaged column(s): primarily **online track** and **charging beads**.  
- What it destroys: **hierarchy** (overview vs execution), and the boundary between **normal pages (flow/stages)** and **exception/constraint pages (locks/ops loops)**, because the “pretty” diagram is not a substitute for lifecycle/stage gates.

**[Box 4 — Minimal revision to reduce risk]**  
Keep the eye‑catching page as the “cover card” but add:
1) A fixed strip under it: “You must also pass: P9 (steps) → P10 (roadmap fields)”.  
2) Two explicit callouts on the diagram: “Costs live in charging beads (P10)” and “Stages live in online track (P7/P9)”.  
This preserves the main line while letting the diagram be a representative *entrance* only.

---

## B) Merging **user sticker** and **charging beads** because “same direction, different angles”
**Decision: must be returned**

**[Box 1 — Why people want this]**  
Both feel like “business stuff” rather than technical flow: “target market segment” (P5) and “Estimated Budget / BUs involved” (P10) look like management overlays, so people want a single “commercial” column.

**[Box 2 — Narrow conditions where it can stand]**  
Only if the merged column is **explicitly split internally** into two non-substitutable sections with separate gates:  
- Section 1: **who** (user sticker: target segment / roles)  
- Section 2: **how much** (charging beads: budget/revenue/billing)  
But that is functionally *not a merge*; it’s a re-labeling. With your rule “don’t change column names”, a true merge breaks the site.

**[Box 3 — What’s missing / which column gets damaged]**  
- Missing: the material itself keeps them separated: **P5** isolates “Target market segment” as a design block; **P10** isolates “Estimated Budget” and “Departments/3rd parties”.  
- Damaged column(s): both **user sticker** and **charging beads** lose boundary integrity; downstream it damages **dependency lock** because prerequisites become ambiguous (“do we need segment defined or budget approved first?”).  
- What it destroys: **role division** and **resource allocation**. “User sticker” answers *who/for whom*; “charging beads” answers *money/revenue/billing/budget*. Combining collapses two different prerequisite types into one, making later gates impossible to enforce.

**[Box 4 — Minimal revision to reduce risk]**  
Don’t merge. Instead add a **cross-link rule**:  
- Every user sticker assertion must point to the charging bead it impacts (e.g., “target segment” → “estimated budget / billing”).  
- Keep separate columns but add a small “binding tag” like `Sticker→Beads` on the relevant pages (P5 ↔ P10, P7↔P10).

---

## C) Using **dependency lock / online track** (limitations/exceptions) at the beginning to omit intermediate steps
**Decision: can only be partially retained**

**[Box 1 — Why people want this]**  
They believe stating constraints first (fault/performance loops in **P7**, approvals/cross-dept in **P9**) prevents wasted work and allows skipping steps.

**[Box 2 — Narrow conditions where it can stand]**  
It can stand only as a **pre-flight checklist** placed before the main line, not as the main narrative start. That checklist must be short and must reference the normal flow it guards. Example: a one-screen lock list pointing to **P4/P5/P6** (what you’re locking).

**[Box 3 — What’s missing / which column gets damaged]**  
- Missing: the object being constrained. If you start with locks, you haven’t established “content/platform/experience/segment” (P4/P5) or “capabilities chain” (P6).  
- Damaged column(s): **service grid** gets undermined because “what we are building” is not defined before “what can go wrong / what must be approved”.  
- What it destroys: the relationship between **normal pages and exception pages**. In the material, P7’s fault/performance blocks are explicitly embedded inside a larger lifecycle—those are *exceptions/loops inside a normal flow*, not the opening statement of the product.

**[Box 4 — Minimal revision to reduce risk]**  
Add a single “Lock Banner” at the top of the entry (P1/P3 area):  
- “Before execution (P9/P10), confirm: cross-dept approvals exist + ops loop exists (P7).”  
Then proceed in the normal order (P4→P5→P6→P9→P10). This keeps locks early without letting them replace the flow.

## D) Using the rear finishing/settlement/summary page to determine the previous actions (reverse-driving the flow)
**Decision: can only be partially retained**

**[Box 1 — Why people want this]**  
**P10** is a form-like template (Strategic focus, KPIs, BUs, Budget, context/benefits). People want to start from it because it looks actionable and measurable.

**[Box 2 — Narrow conditions where it can stand]**  
It can stand only if treated as a **blank form** used to *collect unknowns*, not to *declare completed decisions*. It must be explicitly marked “draft placeholder; values will be filled after P4–P9.”

**[Box 3 — What’s missing / which column gets damaged]**  
- Missing: P10 references fields that require upstream definitions: “Strategic focus area”, “Contributing KPIs”, “Departments/3rd parties”, “Estimated Budget”. The deck does not show how to populate these without the earlier framework and steps.

**[Box 4 — Minimal revision to reduce risk]**  
Allow P10 at the beginning only as an “Intake Sheet” with three explicit statuses per field: `{unknown | assumed | validated}` and a mandatory pointer to where it gets validated:

## E) Concluding two pages are the same object based on same noun / similar diagram / same platform or org name
**Decision: must be returned**

**[Box 1 — Why people want this]**  
The deck reuses the same nouns and visuals (e.g., **P4** and **P5** share the same CVP block layout; multiple pages mention operator/platform/billing/customer). People equate repeated labels with identical purpose.

**[Box 2 — Narrow conditions where it can stand]**

**[Box 3 — What’s missing / which column gets damaged]**

  - P7 “Billing and Revenue Management” is lifecycle/ops;  
  - P6 “Billing and collection” is a delivery capability icon;  
  - P10 “Estimated Budget” is planning cost.  
  Same money noun, three different columns/timepoints.  
- Damaged column(s): all, but especially **online track** vs **charging beads** vs **service grid**—object identity gets flattened and pages get wrongly merged.  
- What it destroys: **hierarchy** (overview vs detail), and **conditional boundaries** (design object vs operational stage vs budgeting artifact).

**[Box 4 — Minimal revision to reduce risk]**  
Introduce a forced labeling convention on each page card:  
- `Object-type:` {framework block | design block | capability | lifecycle stage | template field}  
- `Time-point:` {design | build | operate | plan/portfolio}

# Danger ranking (1 = most dangerous → 5 = least dangerous)

1) **E** — Most dangerous: it causes uncontrolled **false merging** across the entire system (same noun ⇒ same object), collapsing **hierarchy** and **conditional boundaries** everywhere. This is enough to divert the main line because it will “prove” (incorrectly) that you can skip required transitions (e.g., treat P6 billing icon as equivalent to P10 budget or P7 revenue management), destroying the site’s column logic.

2) **B** — Collapsing **user sticker** into **charging beads** breaks **role division** and **resource allocation**. It makes prerequisites ambiguous (segment decision vs budget approval), so gates stop functioning.

3) **C** — Starting with locks/exceptions flips **normal vs exception**. It can erase the service grid definition step and encourages skipping intermediate build blocks, producing a brittle flow.

4) **D** — Reverse-driving from the ending template confuses **completion status** (draft vs validated). It can still be contained if you mark fields as unknown/assumed/validated.

5) **A** — Least dangerous: mainly a **presentation shortcut** problem. If you keep the “eye-catching page” as an entrance with mandatory links, it stays a local framing issue rather than a structural collapse of roles/timepoints/conditions.
